title: Qualcomm's Two-Dollar Jury Award Positions Delaware Judge to Suspend Arm Royalties
subtitle: A split verdict turns commercial friction into legal leverage ahead of Oct. 20 closing arguments.
summary: A federal jury awarded Qualcomm nominal damages after finding Arm breached its core architecture license agreement. The technical victory gives a federal judge the opening to suspend Qualcomm's royalty payments for five years.

bodyHtml:
A two-dollar verdict is usually the legal system's way of telling you that you are technically right and nobody cares. When a federal jury in Delaware handed Qualcomm exactly two one-dollar bills on October 13, it was easy to mistake the award for a punchline. But that nominal sum is not a damages payout; it is a skeleton key.

The Numbers That Matter

Qualcomm designs the microscopic brains that power your smartphone. Think of Arm as the architect who draws the floor plans, while Qualcomm buys the raw blueprint and builds an entire custom mansion on top of it. The business runs on two distinct machines. QCT builds and sells physical silicon, from Snapdragon mobile processors to modem chips. QTL is an intellectual-property toll booth, collecting high-margin checks on virtually every cellular device shipped on Earth. Qualcomm relies on an architecture license agreement to craft bespoke Oryon computing cores rather than leasing pre-made designs off the shelf, keeping costs down and margins high.

That design freedom is why this fight exists. Arm, backed by SoftBank, wants to move up the food chain from selling blueprints to hawking finished chips, launching its own silicon earlier this year and clashing directly with its biggest client.

The Delaware jury split the difference across six claims, handing Arm four victories regarding standard licensing terms while finding Arm liable for two crucial violations. Specifically, the jury found Arm breached its core architecture contract by withholding critical technical deliverables for over two years. It also found Arm interfered with Qualcomm’s commercial relationship with Meta Platforms, by leaking a termination threat across the industry.

Those two breach findings instantly reshape the balance of power. While the jury handled contract liability, Judge Maryellen Noreika is presiding over a parallel bench proceeding that decides the actual remedies. Under a specific enforcement clause in the architecture agreement, Qualcomm argues that Arm’s contractual breach entitles it to halt royalty payments entirely for up to five years. Closing arguments arrive on October 20, and Reuters estimates that relief could reach into the billions.

Here is why that mechanism matters to the equity. For a stock trading roughly a third below its late-May highs, an input-cost reset of this scale is completely unpriced. If Judge Noreika enforces the contract clause, the cost of the underlying instruction set inside every flagship Snapdragon chip drops to zero for half a decade. That margin windfall would flow straight to the bottom line, providing massive operating leverage precisely as Qualcomm fights through a challenging smartphone replacement cycle.

The equity market treated the jury split as meaningless courtroom noise, but Qualcomm quietly demonstrated relative strength by outperforming the broader semiconductor index as the sector sold off last week. Investors have spent months punishing Qualcomm for consumer phone fatigue and the looming loss of modem supply to Apple. They have ignored the fact that Qualcomm's trial counsel did not sue to collect a check, but to construct a legal crowbar before the bench.

A short seller, however, would look at the two-dollar award and point out that the jury found zero commercial damage. Punitive contract clauses that wipe out years of fees face an uphill battle under California law, and Arm is making exactly that case: the five-year holiday, it says, is an unenforceable penalty.

Even if Qualcomm escapes paying Arm for five years, its core engine is stalling. Handset chip sales plunged 20% year over year in the June quarter to $5.09 billion. That is still over half of total revenue. Meanwhile, Qualcomm’s grand push to challenge traditional PCs with custom silicon accounts for less than 1% of the PC market excluding tablets. If Judge Noreika strikes down the penalty remedy, Qualcomm remains chained to an architecture partner that doubles as an aggressive competitor.

What we are watching is Judge Noreika’s bench ruling following October 20 closing arguments, followed by management's commentary during fiscal fourth-quarter earnings on November 4. If the court validates the royalty holiday, Qualcomm transforms a nominal two-dollar slap on the wrist into a royalty holiday worth billions.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in QCOM. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
